original_value: AbstractIntellectual contribution in the form of authorship is a fundamental component of the academic career. While research has addressed questionable and harmful authorship practices, there has largely been no discussion of how U.S. academic institutions interpret and potentially mitigate such practices through the use of institution-level authorship policies. To gain a better understanding of the role of U.S. academic institutions in authorship practices, we conducted a systematic review of publicly available authorship policies for U.S. doctoral institutions (using the 266 2018 Carnegie-classified R1 and R2 Universities), focusing on components such as specification of authorship criteria, recommendations for discussing authorship, dispute resolution processes, and guidance for faculty-student collaborations. We found that only 24% of the 266 Carnegie R1 and R2 Universities had publicly available authorship policies. Within these policies, the majority (93%) specified criteria for authorship, but provided less guidance about actual processes for applying such criteria (62%), handling authorship disputes (62%), and managing faculty-student author teams (49%). Further, we found that any discussion of dispute resolution practices typically lacked specificity. Recommendations grounded in these findings are offered for institutions to leverage their ability to guide the authorship process by adopting an authorship policy that acknowledges disciplinary diversity while still offering substantive guidance.

result.paraphrase: Authorship as a form of intellectual contribution is a core part of an academic career. Although prior research has examined dubious and harmful authorship practices, little attention has been paid to how U.S. academic institutions interpret and potentially reduce such practices through institution-level authorship policies. To better understand the role of U.S. institutions in authorship practices, we systematically reviewed publicly available authorship policies at U.S. doctoral institutions, using the 266 R1 and R2 universities classified by Carnegie in 2018, with attention to authorship criteria, advice on authorship discussions, dispute resolution procedures, and guidance for faculty-student collaborations. We found that only 24% of the 266 Carnegie R1 and R2 universities had publicly available authorship policies. Among those policies, most (93%) defined criteria for authorship, but fewer addressed how to apply those criteria in practice (62%), resolve authorship disputes (62%), or manage faculty-student author teams (49%). We also found that discussions of dispute resolution usually lacked detail. Based on these findings, we provide recommendations for institutions to use their capacity to shape the authorship process by adopting policies that recognize disciplinary diversity while still giving meaningful guidance.
